extracted.intended_audience: researchers/inventors in natural products (Chinese medicine), technology transfer officers, and patent practitioners seeking guidance on US patenting of isolated natural products
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for obtaining and drafting US patents on isolated natural products, their derivatives, formulations, methods of use, product-by-process claims, and related disclosures in view of Myriad/Mayo and USPTO guidance. Targets claim drafting, specification content, and prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility vs patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be new and useful to be patentable in the United States; laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are excluded from patent-eligible protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent eligibility determines whether an invention can seek patent protection (subject-matter), whereas patentability requires meeting novelty, inventiveness (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability. Natural products discovered (not invented) are excluded from patent eligibility even if useful; a non-natural compound is patent-eligible but may be unpatentable if known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / 'markedly different' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated natural product must be 'significantly' or 'markedly' different from what exists in nature to be patent-eligible; mere isolation or purification is not necessarily invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have required that isolation/purification must result in 'properties and characteristics which were different in kind from those of the known product rather than in degree.' Examples: recrystallized aspirin and purified adrenalin deemed patentable (therapeutically different); purified tungsten and certain bacterial strains found unpatentable (commercial usefulness attributed to intrinsic properties). Absence of a robust standard for 'in kind' vs 'in degree' creates uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Myriad decision on isolated genetic/natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad held that an isolated DNA molecule with an identical sequence to a natural gene is not patentable as it is a naturally-occurring product; complementary DNA (cDNA) with introns removed can be patentable, though short strands indistinguishable from natural DNA may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court found that severing chemical bonds to isolate DNA did not create 'markedly different characteristics' and emphasized that claims focused on genetic information (naturally occurring) are not created by patentees. Apply analogously to other isolated natural molecules: structural identity to natural counterpart weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2014 guidance: weighting factors and 'marked difference' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance provides a list of factors for and against patent eligibility of claims involving natural principles/products and determines eligibility principally by whether the claim recites something 'significantly' or 'markedly' different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points from guidance: 'a marked difference must be a significant difference, i.e., more than an incidental or trivial difference.' Structural differences are a primary (but not sole) criterion; functional differences can be considered when structural differences are absent; words like 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight. Examples: synthetic derivative 5-methyl amazonic acid is patent-eligible (structural difference); purified amazonic acid is not (no marked difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural difference favored over mere functional difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural difference is deemed sufficient for patent eligibility, whereas a functional (utility) difference is not mandatory and may or may not weigh in chemical/natural product cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structural difference is absent or insignificant, the claimed natural product must exhibit new functions/characteristics that rise to the level of 'marked' differences. Functional differences alone do not guarantee eligibility; assess whether they are 'marked' beyond routine or incidental benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition/combination claims of natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions combining multiple natural products remain products of nature if the combined products show no marked difference from the natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositions may be patent-eligible if they include additional element(s) that make the combination 'something significantly different than the natural products by themselves' — e.g., enhanced efficacy at a lower dosage. Draft and support combination claims with evidence of markedly different properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-use claims must recite practical, specific, significant application
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of using natural products should involve a practical, specific, and significant application so the claimed method would not foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that merely recite: (i) a general instruction to apply or use the natural products; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that need to be used by anyone who applies the natural products. Include additional steps such as regimen and dosage (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid for 10–20 days at a daily dose of 0.76–1.25 teaspoons') to satisfy the requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table summary: likely patentability outcomes under USPTO policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the USPTO policy, extracts and isolated products from natural materials are likely to be unpatentable; formulations of combined extracts may be patentable if 'markedly different'; manufacturing methods are patentable if they meet novelty and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this high-level mapping to prioritize claim drafting: focus less on isolated per se claims and more on derivatives, formulations, methods, and applications that can be shown to be different in kind or provide marked advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim constraints in the US
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Product-by-process' claims define a product by the process used to make it (e.g., “product X obtained by process Y”) and are allowed when products cannot otherwise be adequately defined, but US patentability of such claims is determined solely on the product itself, not the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product identical or similar to a known product is not patentable even if made by a new method. Process steps are considered only if they imply distinctive structural characteristics. Product-by-process claims may be limited in enforcement (they only cover products produced by the recited process) and may not cover equivalents made by different processes; accused products made by a different process may not infringe. Recommended practice: include all available characterization in the specification and draft separate product and process claims for broader protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on novelty/non-obviousness for claimed product similar to known products
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed product is identical to, or similar to, a known product, applicants bear the burden of proof on novelty and non-obviousness to show the claimed product is distinguishable from known products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide structural/functional evidence and characterization to meet this burden. If such proof is available, the product may be adequately defined (which paradoxically undermines the need for product-by-process language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement/infringement limitations for product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Product-by-process' claims only cover products that are produced by the process recited in the claim; an accused product made by a different process does not infringe such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits the scope of protection from product-by-process claims. Consider drafting both process claims (to capture infringers using the claimed method) and product claims (if possible) and include detailed characterization to avoid reliance solely on product-by-process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / written description and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: US patent law requires sufficient description so that one skilled in the art would recognize the inventions; a claim reciting a general formula is not patentable if only a few species of the general formula are disclosed in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to a general formula (e.g., CnH2n+2) may be limited to species explicitly described (e.g., CH4, C3H8) if only those were disclosed. To obtain broader scope, disclose as many embodiments, substitutions, and variations as possible; include experimental conditions and technical features (temperature, pH, reagents). Claims should be drafted to include all enabling and foreseeable embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting: scope, significance, and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be drafted within a reasonable scope and be of sufficient significance so they do not appear to be a general application of the natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly broad claims that merely apply a natural product generally. Add technical limitations, specific regimens, dosages, modified structures, or unique manufacturing steps to show significance and limit scope. Identify and characterize individual embodiments and combinations for broader coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended patenting strategy for natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus patenting efforts on derivatives with enhanced properties, optimized formulations and dosages, new uses or applications, and advanced methods for preparing natural products; disclose detailed information to meet written description and enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and characterize individual embodiments and/or combinations to support broader claim coverage. Frequently review developments in patenting policy and adjust strategy. Include detailed descriptions in the specification and draft multiple claim sets (product, product-by-process, process, method-of-use) as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing/process claims remain viable
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing methods such as extraction and preparation of drugs/supplements using natural products are patentable if they satisfy statutory requirements like novelty and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when product claims are vulnerable under the product-of-nature doctrine, well-drafted process claims can provide meaningful protection. Ensure processes imparting distinctive structural characteristics are well-supported in the specification.
